verses.zh: 以色列家啊，要听耶和华对你们所说的话。
verses.en: You people of Israel,[NOTE:1] listen to what the Lord has to say to you.
notes: Heb “house of Israel.”
verses.commentary:
10:1 "Hear the word" This is the Hebrew word Shema (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal
IMPERATIVE), which means "to hear so as to do." It is
a recurrent demand in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 2:4; 5:21; 6:19; 7:2,23; 10:1; 11:2,4,6; 13:15; 17:20; 19:3;
21:11; 22:2; 31:10; 38:20; 42:15; 44:24,26; 49:20; 50:45). YHWH is communicating, but His people are
not listening and obeying!

▣ "house of Israel" The title "Israel" in Jeremiah is so confusing because it is used
in two senses.

- all of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob

- the Northern Ten Tribes, who split off in 922 B.C.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：你们不要效法列国的行为，也不要为天象惊惶，因列国为此事惊惶。
verses.en: The Lord says:“Do not start following pagan religious practices.[NOTE:1] Do not be in awe of signs that occur[NOTE:2] in the skyeven though the nations hold them in awe.
notes: Heb “Do not learn the way of the nations.” For this use of the word “ways” (דֶּרֶךְ, derekh) compare, for example, Jer 12:16 and Isa 2:6.

The Hebrew word translated here as “things that go on in the sky” (אֹתוֹת, ʾotot) refers to unusual disturbances such as eclipses, comets, meteors, etc., but also to such things as changes in position of the sun, moon, and stars in conjunction with the changes in seasons (cf. Gen 1:14). The people of Assyria and Babylonia worshiped the sun, moon, and stars, thinking that these heavenly bodies had some hold over them.tn Heb “signs.” The words “that occur” are supplied in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
10:2 "Do not learn the way of the nations" Chapter 10 addresses the folly of idolatry. It reflects
the imagery and sarcasm of Isaiah (cf. Isa. 2:20; 31:7; 40:18-20; 41:7; 44:9-20; 45:16; 46:5-7). YHWH
had given them the way in which they should walk (cf. Lev. 18:3; Deut. 12:30; Jer. 12:16), but they chose the way
(i.e. lifestyle) of idolatry. This is even reflected in Jer. 10:2 by a seeming allusion to the
Babylonian astral deities (i.e. "signs of the heavens," cf. Isa. 47:13; many celestial signs are recorded in
Enuma Anu Enlil).

There are two Qal IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense
(negated).

- learn ‒ BDB 540, KB 531

- be terrified ‒ BDB 369, KB 365

The pagan nations, without a knowledge of YHWH, were terrified (BDB 369, KB 365, Qal
IMPERFECT) by the astrologers (cf. Isa. 47:12-14) and astral events, like meteors, comets,
eclipses, weather phenonema. Superstitions are powerful instruments
in the hand of Satan to frighten, intimidate, and control humans!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

verses.zh: 众民的风俗是虚空的；他们在树林中用斧子砍伐一棵树，匠人用手工造成偶像。
verses.en: For the religion[NOTE:1] of these people is worthless.They cut down a tree in the forest,and a craftsman makes it into an idol with his tools.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “statutes.” According to BDB 350 s.v. חֻקָּה 2.b it refers to the firmly established customs or practices of the pagan nations. Cf. Lev 20:23; 2 Kgs 17:8. Here it is essentially equivalent to דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) in v. 1, which has already been translated “religious practices.”

This passage is dripping with sarcasm. It begins by talking about the “statutes” of the pagan peoples as a “vapor” using a singular copula (הוּא, hu’, “it,” functioning as subject for an understood verb) and singular predicate. Then it suppresses the subject, the idol, as though it were too horrible to mention, using only the predications about it. The last two lines read literally: “for a tree from the forest, one cuts it down, a work of hands of a craftsman with the chisel.”

10:3

NASB
"For the customs of the peoples are

delusion"

NKJV
"For the customs of the peoples

are futile"

NRSV, NJB
"For the customs of the peoples

are false"

worthless"

are a shame"

delusions"

are delusions" (emendation)

The word "customs" (BDB 349) can mean

- to inscribe (i.e. a law)

- to enact or to decree (i.e. a law)

The term "delusion" means "nothingness" or "vanity" (BDB 210, KB 236, cf. Jer. 2:5; 14:22;
2 Kgs. 17:15). It is quite often used to describe the idols (cf. Deut. 32:21), which were nonentities
made by human hands. They had no power to act, in contradistinction to YHWH who acts for His people! Idols
cannot hear, see, or act, but they are used by Satan to trick humans from knowing and following the only
true God and His Messiah (cf. Eph. 6:10-18).

verses.zh: 他们用金银妆饰它，用钉子和锤子钉稳，使它不动摇。
verses.en: He decorates it with overlays of silver and gold.He uses hammer and nails to fasten it[NOTE:1] togetherso that it will not fall over.
notes: The pronoun is plural in Hebrew, referring to the parts.

verses.zh: 它好像棕树，是镟成的，不能说话，不能行走，必须有人抬着。你们不要怕它；它不能降祸，也无力降福。
verses.en: Such idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field.They cannot talk.They must be carried because they cannot walk.Do not be afraid of thembecause they cannot hurt you.And they do not have any power to help you.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “And it is not in them to do good either.”
verses.commentary:
10:5 "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field" This is an allusion to idols described as scarecrows.
Some translate this as "upright as a palm tree" (NKJV, Peshitta). The LXX omits the phrase.

▣ "They must be carried" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT
VERB from the same root (BDB 669, KB 724) used for intensity. Oh, the folly of man-made gods!

▣ "Do not fear them" This is a Qal IMPERFECT (BDB 431, KB 432) used
in a JUSSIVE sense. Fear can be paralyzing!

Notice those who know YHWH should not fear because the idols

- cannot harm you

- cannot do you good

They are non-existent (cf. Isa. 41:23-24; 1 Cor. 8:4; Gal. 4:8). Fear YHWH (cf. Jer. 10:7)!

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，没有能比你的！你本为大，有大能大力的名。
verses.en: I said,[NOTE:1] “There is no one like you, Lord.[NOTE:2] You are great,and you are renowned for your power.[NOTE:3]
notes: The words “I said” are not in the Hebrew text, but there appears to be a shift in speaker. Someone is now addressing the Lord. The likely speaker is Jeremiah, so the words “I said” are supplied in the translation for clarity.

The form that introduces this line has raised debate. The form מֵאֵין (meʾen) normally means “without” and introduces a qualification of a term expressing desolation, or it means “so that not” and introduces a negative result (cf. BDB 35 s.v. II אַיִן 6.b). Neither of these nuances fit either this verse or the occurrence in v. 7. BDB 35 s.v. II אַיִן 6.b.γ notes that some have explained this as a strengthened form of אַיִן (ʾayin), which occurs in a similar phrase five other times (cf., e.g., 1 Kgs 8:23). Though many, including BDB, question the validity of this solution, it is probably better than the suggestion that BDB gives of repointing to מֵאַיִן (meʾayin, “whence”), which scarcely fits the context of v. 7, or the solution of HALOT 41 s.v. I אַיִן, which suggests that the מ (mem) is a double writing (dittograph) of the final consonant from the preceding word. That would assume that the scribe made the same error twice (also in v. 7) or was influenced the second time by the first erroneous writing.
Heb “Great is your name in power.”
verses.commentary:
10:6 "There is none like You" I seems that Jeremiah is speaking. This is an emphasis on the uniqueness of
YHWH. It is an affirmation of monotheism. There was only one God (cf. Jer. 10:10).

The Septuagint omits Jer. 10:6-8 and 10; this omission is also in the Dead Sea Scroll
manuscripts. Possibly these are based on a different Hebrew text.

YHWH (cf. Deut. 3:24; 5:24; 9:26; 11:2; 32:3). Jeremiah often uses the phrasing and terminology from
Deuteronomy.

verses.zh: 万国的王啊，谁不敬畏你？敬畏你本是合宜的；因为在列国的智慧人中，虽有政权的尊荣，也不能比你。
verses.en: Everyone should revere you, O King of all nations,[NOTE:1] because you deserve to be revered.[NOTE:2] For there is no one like youamong any of the wise people of the nations nor among any of their kings.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Who should not revere you…?” The question is rhetorical and expects a negative answer.
Heb “For it is fitting to you.”
Heb “their royalty/dominion.” This is a case of substituting the abstract “royalty, royal power” for the concrete “kings” who exercise it.
verses.commentary:
10:7 "King of the nations" YHWH is not just the God of Abraham's seed but the God of creation! He is
the only true God (cf. Jer. 10:10)!

This emphasis on YHWH as the only true God is difficult to communicate to a post-modern
worldview which depreciates absolutes. Yet, this is the question! It is true or
it is false. The biblical worldview rests on this basic affirmation.

verses.zh: 他们尽都是畜类，是愚昧的。偶像的训诲算甚么呢？偶像不过是木头。
verses.en: The people of those nations[NOTE:1] are both stupid and foolish.Instruction from a wooden idol is worthless![NOTE:2]
notes: Or “Those wise people and kings are…” It is unclear whether the subject is the “they” of the nations in the preceding verse, or the wise people and kings referred to there. The text merely has “they.”

Heb “The instruction of vanities [worthless idols] is wood.” The interpretation of this line is a little uncertain. Various proposals have been made, most of which involve radical emendation of the text. For some examples see J. A. Thompson, Jeremiah (NICOT), 323-24, fn 6. However, this is probably a case of the bold predication discussed in GKC 452 §141.d, some examples of which may be seen in Ps 109:4 (“I am prayer”) and Ps 120:7 (“I am peace”).
verses.commentary:
10:8 This verse is very difficult to translate, but it seems that the Hebrew is referring to the
fact that the Israelites were getting their information and knowledge from a dead stump (i.e. idol).

The second line may be paralleled in v. 3a.

verses.zh: 有银子打成片，是从他施带来的，并有从乌法来的金子，都是匠人和银匠的手工，又有蓝色紫色料的衣服，都是巧匠的工作。
verses.en: Hammered-out silver is brought from Tarshish[NOTE:1] and gold is brought from Ufaz[NOTE:2] to cover those idols.[NOTE:3] They are the handiwork of carpenters and goldsmiths.[NOTE:4] They are clothed in blue and purple clothes.[NOTE:5] They are all made by skillful workers.[NOTE:6]
notes: Two Qumran scrolls of Jeremiah (4QJera and 4QJerb) reflect a Hebrew text that is very different than the traditional MT from which modern Bibles have been translated. The Hebrew text in these two manuscripts is similar to that from which LXX was translated. This is true both in small details and in major aspects where the LXX differs from MT. Most notably, 4QJera, 4QJerb and LXX present a version of Jeremiah about 13% shorter than the longer version found in MT. One example of this shorter text is Jer 10:3-11 in which MT and 4QJera both have all nine verses, while LXX and 4QJerb both lack vv. 6-8 and 10, which extol the greatness of God. In addition, the latter part of v. 9 is arranged differently in LXX and 4QJerb. The translation here follows MT, which is supported by 4QJera.

This is a place of unknown location. It is mentioned again in Dan 10:5. Many emend the word to “Ophir” following the Syriac version and the Aramaic Targum. Ophir was famous for its gold (cf. 1 Kgs 9:28; Job 28:16).
The words “to cover those idols” are not in the text but are implicit from the context. They are supplied in the translation for clarity.
The words “They are” are not in the text. The text reads merely, “the work of the carpenter and of the hands of the goldsmith.” The words are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Blue and purple their clothing.”

There is an ironic pun in this last line. The Hebrew word translated “skillful workers” is the same word that is translated “wise people” in v. 7. The artisans do their work skillfully but they are not “wise.”
verses.commentary:
10:9 "Tarshish" This was a city in the far west, possibly Spain or Sardinia. Some say it is just
a mythological place to describe something far, far away (cf. the book of Jonah and Ezek. 27:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH

▣ "And gold from Uphaz" "from Uphaz" (מאופז, BDB 20) is found
only here and in Dan. 10:5 as a place name. From 1 Kgs. 9:28 a place called "from Ophir"
(פאופיר, BDB 20, cf. Isa. 13:12) has "gold" (cf. Targums, Peshitta,
REB). It possibly means "pure" or "fine" gold, thereby functioning as an ADJECTIVVE.

▣ "Violet and purple are their clothing" These were very expensive dyes in the ancient world,
originally coming from Phoenicia (i.e. from sea shells). It is simply a way of asserting that no matter how richly or royally
they robed their idols, they were still just human-made, inanimate objects!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE SACRED COLORS

▣ "They are all the work of skilled men" The NET Bible (p. 1316, #17) points out the contrast
between

- the wise men of the nations

- the skilled craftsmen

Both use the same root (BDB 314). These idol makers are skillful craftsmen, but they are not
wise. True wisdom cannot worship a man-made idol!

verses.zh: （你们要对他们如此说：不是那创造天地的神，必从地上从天下被除灭！）
verses.en: You people of Israel should tell those nations this:‘These gods did not make heaven and earth.They will disappear[NOTE:1] from the earth and from under the heavens.’[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “The gods who did not make…earth will disappear…” In conformity with contemporary English style, the sentence is broken up in the translation to avoid a long, complex English sentence.

This passage is carefully structured and placed to contrast the Lord, who is living and eternal (v. 10) and made the heavens and earth (v. 12), with the idols, who did not and will disappear. It also has a very careful, concentric structure in the original text where “the gods” is balanced by “these,” “heavens” by “from under the heavens,” and “the earth” by “from the earth.” In the very center, “did not make” is balanced and contrasted by “will disappear.” The structure is further reinforced by the sound play/wordplay between “did not make” (Aram לָא עֲבַדוּ [laʾ ʿavadu]) and “will disappear” (Aram יֵאבַדוּ [yeʾvadu]). This is the rhetorical climax of Jeremiah’s sarcastic attack on the folly of idolatry.tn This verse is in Aramaic. It is the only Aramaic sentence in Jeremiah. Scholars debate the appropriateness of this verse to this context. Many see it as a gloss added by a postexilic scribe that was later incorporated into the text. Both R. E. Clendenen (“Discourse Strategies in Jeremiah 10, ” JBL 106 [1987]: 401-8) and W. L. Holladay (Jeremiah [Hermeneia], 1:324-25, 334-35) have given detailed arguments that the passage is not only original but the climax and center of the contrast between the Lord and idols in vv. 2-16. God gives Israel a message for the nations in the lingua franca of the time. Holladay shows that the passage is a very carefully constructed chiasm (see accompanying study note). This fact argues that “these” at the end is the subject of the verb “will disappear,” not an attributive adjective modifying heaven. He also makes a very good case that the verse is poetry and not the prose that it is rendered in the majority of modern English versions.
verses.commentary:
10:11 This verse is in Aramaic. It is the only verse in Jeremiah in Aramaic (also note
Ezra 4:8-6:18; 7:12-26; Dan. 2:4-7:28). Why one Aramaic verse should appear in the midst of a Hebrew
book is uncertain. Some of the theories are:

- The rabbis say that it was part of a letter sent to King Jehoiachin in captivity in Neo-Babylon.

- It was an anti-polytheistic proverb.

- It was an exorcism formula (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: EXORCISM)

- It was a marginal note, later inserted into the text (TEV, NEB).

verses.zh: 耶和华用能力创造大地，用智慧建立世界，用聪明铺张穹苍。
verses.en: The Lord is the one who[NOTE:1] by his power made the earth.He is the one who by his wisdom established the world.And by his understanding, he spread out the skies.
notes: The words “The Lord is” are not in the text. They are implicit from the context. They are supplied in the translation here because of possible confusion about who the subject is due to the parenthetical address to the people of Israel in v. 11. The first two verbs are participles and should not merely be translated as the narrative past. They are predicate nominatives of an implied copula intending to contrast the Lord, as the one who made the earth, with the idols, which did not.
verses.commentary:
10:12-16 This is a passage about Elohim as creator of both the planet and all celestial objects (cf. Gen. 1:14-19).
In this passage it is He who gives and controls water, which was a very important theological issue in the agricultural Ancient
Near East. Water was part of the Neo-Babylonian creation myth and the Canaanite creation myth. The Canaanite god, Ba'al,
was supposedly the storm god that provided water (i.e. life). Contrary to both of these myths, YHWH is the creator, sustainer,
and provider of rain and water.

Who established the world by His wisdom" This is an emphasis on God as

This is possibly the OT background for John 1:1-14.

verses.zh: 他一发声，空中便有多水激动；他使云雾从地极上腾；他造电随雨而闪，从他府库中带出风来。
verses.en: When his voice thunders,[NOTE:1] the heavenly ocean roars.He makes the clouds rise from the far-off horizons.[NOTE:2] He makes the lightning flash out in the midst of the rain.He unleashes the wind from the places where he stores it.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “At the voice of his giving.” The idiom “to give the voice” is often used for thunder (cf. BDB 679 s.v. נָתַן Qal.1.x).
Heb “from the ends of the earth.”
Heb “he brings out the winds from his storehouses.”
verses.commentary:
10:13 This verse may be a parody of the Canaanite fertility god, Ba'al, who was the storm god.
YHWH is the One who controls water and the weather, not Ba'al.

verses.zh: 各人都成了畜类，毫无知识；各银匠都因他雕刻的偶像羞愧。他所铸的偶像本是虚假的，其中并无气息，
verses.en: All these idolaters[NOTE:1] will prove to be stupid and ignorant.Every goldsmith will be disgraced by the idol he made.For the image he forges is merely a sham.[NOTE:2] There is no breath in any of those idols.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Every man.” But in the context this is not a reference to all people without exception but to all idolaters. The referent is made explicit for the sake of clarity.
Or “nothing but a phony god”; Heb “a lie/falsehood.”
Heb “There is no breath in them.” The referent is made explicit so that no one will mistakenly take it to refer to the idolaters or goldsmiths.
verses.commentary:
10:14-15 These verses continue the ridicule of idols (cf. Jer. 10:3-5). The term "breath" (BDB 924) is a play
on the term for spirit (cf. Ezekiel 37).

verses.zh: 都是虚无的，是迷惑人的工作；到追讨的时候必被除灭。
verses.en: They are worthless, mere objects to be mocked.[NOTE:1] When the time comes to punish them, they will be destroyed.
notes: Or “objects of mockery.”

verses.zh: 雅各的分不像这些，因他是造作万有的主。以色列也是他产业的支派，万军之耶和华是他的名。
verses.en: The Lord, who is the inheritance[NOTE:1] of Jacob’s descendants,[NOTE:2] is not like them.He is the one who created everything.And the people of Israel are those he claims as his own.[NOTE:3] His name is the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.”[NOTE:4]
notes: In the phrase the inheritance of Jacob’s descendants, “inheritance” could be translated “portion.” Applied to God here, the phrase has its background in Joshua’s division of the land of Canaan (Palestine), where each tribe received a land portion except the tribe of Levi, whose “portion” was the Lord. As the other tribes lived off what their portion of the land provided, the tribe of Levi lived off what the Lord provided, i.e., the tithes and offerings dedicated to him. Hence to have the Lord as one’s portion, one’s inheritance, is to have him provide for all one’s needs (see Ps 16:5 in the context of vv. 2, 6, and Lam 3:24 in the context of vv. 22-23).tn The words “The Lord who is” are not in the text. They are supplied in the translation for clarity. For the significance of the words after them see the study note that follows.
Heb “The Portion of Jacob.” “Descendants” is implied, and is supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “And Israel is the tribe of his possession.”
For this rendering of the name for God and its significance see 2:19 and the study note there.tn Heb “Yahweh of Armies.”
verses.commentary:
10:16 "The portion of Jacob is not like these" This refers to the God of Jacob (cf. Ps. 73:26).
Jacob's name was changed to Israel (cf. Gen. 32:28).

▣ "Israel is the tribe of His inheritance" The KJV has "the rod of His inheritance." This
refers to the rod as a means of measurement or a standard (see BDB 986). However, most English
translations follow NASB. Israel is YHWH's own people.

verses.en: “Gather your belongings together and prepare to leave the land,you people of Jerusalem[NOTE:1] who are being besieged.[NOTE:2]
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

Heb “you who are living in/under siege.” The pronouns in this verse are feminine singular in Hebrew. Jerusalem is being personified as a single woman. This personification carries on down through v. 19, where she speaks in the first person. It is difficult, however, to reflect this in a meaningful translation without being somewhat paraphrastic like this.
verses.commentary:
10:17-18 This strophe starts with an IMPERATIVE, "pick up your bundle" (BDB 62,
KB 72, Qal IMPERATIVE) which denotes the imminence of the Neo-Babylonian exile. It
shows that the Judean people would go into exile with only that which they could carry; that YHWH is
the One who pronounced this judgment because of their sin, not because Marduk was a greater and
stronger deity!

verses.zh: 因为耶和华如此说：这时候，我必将此地的居民，好像用机弦甩出去，又必加害在他们身上，使他们觉悟。
verses.en: For the Lord says, ‘I will now throw outthose who live in this land.I will bring so much trouble on themthat they will actually feel it.’[NOTE:1]
notes: The meaning of this last line is somewhat uncertain: Heb “I will cause them distress in order that [or with the result that] they will find.” The absence of an object for the verb “find” has led to conjecture that the text is wrong. Some commentators follow the lead of the Greek and Latin versions which read the verb as a passive: “they will be found,” i.e., be caught and captured. Others follow a suggestion by G. R. Driver (“Linguistic and Textual Problems: Jeremiah,” JQR 28 [1937-38]: 107) that the verb be read not as “they will find” (יִמְצָאוּ [yimtsaʾu] from מָצָא [matsaʾ]) but “they will be squeezed/ drained” (יִמְצוּ [yimtsu] from מָצָה [matsah]). The translation adopted assumes that this is an example of the ellipsis of the object supplied from the context (cf. E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 8-12). For a similar nuance for the verb “find” = “feel/experience” see BDB 592 s.v. מָצָא Qal.1.f and compare the usage in Ps 116:3.
verses.commentary:
10:18 The last line has several translation options.

NASB
"that they may be found"

MT, NKJV
"that they may find it so"

(from מצא, BDB 592)

NRSV, Peshitta
"that they may find me!"

TEV
"until not one is left"

NJB, JPSOA, NET Bible
"that they shall feel it"

LXX
"that your plague may be

discovered"

REB, NEB
"squeeze them dry"

(from מצה, BDB 594)

NIV
"that they may be captured"

JPSOA (footnte)
"that they have to leave"

(emendation)

Apparently the line refers to the fact that none shall escape capture and exile. Literary context
(i.e. Hebrew parallelism) and word root (i.e. Semitic) are the two most helpful ways to determine meaning
of a word or phrase in poetry.

verses.zh: 民说：祸哉！我受损伤；我的伤痕极其重大。我却说：这真是我的痛苦，必须忍受。
verses.en: And I cried out,[NOTE:1] ‘We are doomed![NOTE:2] Our wound is severe!’We once thought, ‘This is only an illness.And we will be able to bear it.’[NOTE:3]
notes: The words “And I cried out” are not in the text. It is not altogether clear who the speaker is in vv. 19-25. The words of vv. 19-20 would best be assigned to a personified Jerusalem who laments the destruction of her city (under the figure of a tent) and the exile of her citizens (under the figure of children). However, the words of v. 21, which assign responsibility to the rulers, do not fit well in the mouth of the people but do fit Jeremiah. The words of v. 22 are very appropriate to Jeremiah, being similar to the report in 4:19-20. Likewise, the words of v. 23, which appear to express man’s incapacity to control his own destiny and his resignation to the fate which awaits him, in the light of v. 24 seem more appropriate to Jeremiah than to the people. There has been no indication elsewhere that the people are resigned to their fate or willing to accept their punishment. Though the issue is far from resolved, a majority of commentators see Jeremiah as the speaker, so identifying himself with their fate that he speaks as though he were this personified figure. It is not altogether out of the question, however, that the speaker throughout is personified Jerusalem, though no known commentator takes that view. For those who are interested, the most thorough discussion of the issue is probably found in W. McKane, Jeremiah (ICC), 1:230-35, especially 233-35. Rendering the pronouns throughout as “we” and “our” alleviates some of the difficulty, but some speaker needs to be identified in the introduction to allay any possible confusion. Hence I have opted for what is the majority view.

Heb “Woe to me on account of my wound.” The words “woe to” in many contexts carry the connotation of hopelessness and of inevitable doom (cf. 1 Sam 4:7, 8; Isa 6:5), hence a “deadly blow.” See also the usage in 4:13, 31; 6:4 and the notes on 4:13. For the rendering of the pronouns as “we” and “our” here and in the verses to follow see the preceding note.

Some interpret this as a resignation to the punishment inflicted and translate, “But I said, ‘This is my punishment, and I will just need to bear it.’” This is unlikely given the meaning and usage of the word rendered “sickness” (חֳלִי, kholi), the absence of the pronoun “my,” and the likelihood that the particle אַךְ (ʾak) means “only” rather than “indeed” (cf. BDB s.v. אַךְ 2.b and compare its usage in v. 24).sn What is being referred to here is the feeling, encouraged by the false prophets, that the ill fortunes of the nation were just temporary setbacks and everything would soon get better (cf. 6:14; 8:11).
verses.commentary:
10:19-22 This strophe of lament is similar to Jer. 8:18-22. It seems to reflect the heart of
God through the words of Jeremiah. However, the nation is personified. The land suffers from mankind's
sin (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28; Rom. 8:18-22). There is a series of nomadic imagery here, particularly
related to the "tent" and "flocks."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

10:19 Jeremiah uses sickness or wounds as imagery for sin (cf. Jer. 30:17), as does
Isaiah 1:5-6; 53:5; Ps. 103:3 (note the synonymous parallelism). These verses cannot be used as a
divine promise of physical healing. However, God still heals.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

▣ The last line of Jer. 10:19 can have several translation options (i.e. different vowels).

NASB, NKJV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta
"I must bear it"

NRSV
"If this is the worst,

I can bear it"

TEV
"we thought this was

something we could

endure!"

LXX
"it seized me"

Number 1 is the people's resignation to Divine judgment. Number 2 is a belittling of the
judgment. I think #1 fits the context best.

verses.zh: 我的帐棚毁坏；我的绳索折断。我的儿女离我出去，没有了。无人再支搭我的帐棚，挂起我的幔子。
verses.en: But our tents have been destroyed.The ropes that held them in place have been ripped apart.[NOTE:1] Our children are gone and are not coming back.[NOTE:2] There is no survivor to put our tents back up,no one left to hang their tent curtains in place.
notes: Heb “My tent has been destroyed and my tent cords have been ripped apart.” For a very similar identification of Jeremiah’s plight with the plight of the personified community, see 4:20 and the notes there.

Heb “my children have gone from me and are no more.”sn What is being referred to is the exile of the people of the land. This passage could refer to the exiles of 605 b.c. or 597 b.c. but more probably anticipates the exile of 588 b.c., since the “tent,” (i.e., the city) is pictured as torn down. The picture of devastation and desolation here should be contrasted with that in Isa 54:2-3.
verses.commentary:
10:20 Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 13, makes the interesting point about how the poets
and prophets used imagery from the nomadic period of Israel's past.

- death as a tent being taken down ‒ Job 4:21

- security as a tent well grounded ‒ Isa. 33:20

- Hezekiah's illness described as a tent being pulled up ‒ Isa. 38:12

- restoration of the covenant people as the enlargement of a tent ‒ Isa. 54:2

- Judah's invasion and exile as a destroyed tent ‒ Jer. 4:20; 10:20

- shepherd imagery ‒ Ps. 23; Isa. 40:11; Jer. 10:21; 23:1-6; Ezek. 34; Zech. 10-12

Only people familiar with nomadic existence can feel the full power and plight of this imagery!

verses.zh: 因为牧人都成为畜类，没有求问耶和华，所以不得顺利；他们的羊群也都分散。
verses.en: For our leaders[NOTE:1] are stupid.They have not sought the Lord’s advice.[NOTE:2] So they do not act wisely,and the people they are responsible for[NOTE:3] have all been scattered.
notes: Heb “the shepherds.”

Heb “They have not sought the Lord.”sn The idiom translated sought the Lord’s advice quite commonly refers to seeking the Lord’s guidance through a prophet. See for example Exod 18:15; 1 Sam 9:9; 1 Kgs 22:8. It would not exclude consulting the law.

Heb “all their flock (or “pasturage”).”sn This verse uses the figure of shepherds for rulers, and that of sheep for the people ruled. It is a common figure in the Bible. See Ezek 34 for an extended development of this metaphor.

verses.zh: 有风声！看哪，敌人来了！有大扰乱从北方出来，要使犹大城邑变为荒凉，成为野狗的住处。
verses.en: Listen! News is coming even now.[NOTE:1] The rumble of a great army is heard approaching[NOTE:2] from a land in the north.[NOTE:3] It is coming to turn the towns of Judah into rubble,places where only jackals live.
notes: Heb “The sound of a report, behold, it is coming.”
Heb “coming, even a great quaking.”
Cf. Jer 6:22.
verses.commentary:
10:22 "A great commotion out of the land of the north" This refers to the coming exile (cf. Jer. 1:14-15;
4:6; 6:1,22). The north was an idiom for invasion since this was the only route that invaders from the Fertile Crescent
(i.e. Mesopotamia) could take because of the desert directly to the east of Palestine.

▣ "A desolation, a haunt of jackals" This line of poetry is asserting two realities.

- the coming invasion and destruction of Judah's walled cities

- the demonic presence in the ruins (i.e. Isa. 34:11-15; Jer. 9:10

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，我晓得人的道路不由自己，行路的人也不能定自己的脚步。
verses.en: Lord, we know that people do not control their own destiny.[NOTE:1] It is not in their power to determine what will happen to them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Not to the man his way.” For the nuance of “fate, destiny, or the way things turn out” for the Hebrew word “way,” see Hag 1:5, Isa 40:27 and probably Ps 49:13 (cf. KBL 218 s.v. דֶּרֶךְ 5). For the idea of “control” or “hold in one’s power” for the preposition “to,” see Ps 3:8 (cf. BDB 513 s.v. לְ 5.b[a]).
Heb “Not to a man the walking and the establishing his step.”
verses.commentary:
10:23-25 This is a closing prayer for mercy as the prophet speaks on behalf of the people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

10:23 "a man's way is not in himself;

Nor is it in a man who walks to direct his steps" This is an affirmation of the
truth that God is in control of all things. There is no place to begin a theology except the sovereignty of the Creator
God! Humans must trust in Him (cf. Prov. 3:5,6; Ps. 37:23; 66:8,9), for there is no one else to trust!

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你从宽惩治我，不要在你的怒中惩治我，恐怕使我归于无有。
verses.en: Correct us, Lord, but only in due measure.[NOTE:1] Do not punish us in anger, or you will reduce us to nothing.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “with justice.”
The words, “to almost nothing” are not in the text. They are implicit from the general context and are supplied by almost all English versions.
verses.commentary:
10:24 "Correct me, O Lord" This is a Piel IMPERATIVE, SINGULAR
(BDB 415, KB 418, used in a collective sense, i.e. "us"). It is the emphasis on God as parent (cf. Prov. 3:12; Ps. 103:6-14;
Heb. 12:5-13). God is a disciplining parent; He disciplines for the purpose of maturity in righteousness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FATHERHOOD OF GOD

verses.zh: 愿你将忿怒倾在不认识你的列国中，和不求告你名的各族上；因为他们吞了雅各，不但吞了，而且灭绝，把他的住处变为荒场。
verses.en: Vent your anger on the nations that do not acknowledge you.[NOTE:1] Vent it on the peoples[NOTE:2] who do not worship you.[NOTE:3] For they have destroyed the people of Jacob.[NOTE:4] They have completely destroyed them[NOTE:5] and left their homeland in utter ruin.”
notes: Heb “know you.” For this use of the word “know” (יָדַע, yadaʿ) see the note on 9:3.
Heb “tribes/clans.”

Heb “who do not call on your name.” The idiom “to call on your name” (directed to God) refers to prayer (mainly) and praise. See 1 Kgs 18:24-26 and Ps 116:13, 17. Here “calling on your name” is parallel to “acknowledging you.” In many locations in the OT “name” is equivalent to the person. In the OT, the “name” reflected the person’s character (cf. Gen 27:36; 1 Sam 25:25) or his reputation (Gen 11:4; 2 Sam 8:13). To speak in a person’s name was to act as his representative or carry his authority (1 Sam 25:9; 1 Kgs 21:8). To call someone’s name over something was to claim it for one’s own (2 Sam 12:28).
Heb “have devoured Jacob.”

Or “have almost completely destroyed them”; Heb “they have devoured them and consumed them.” The figure of hyperbole is used here; elsewhere Jeremiah and God refer to the fact that they will not be completely consumed. See for example 4:27; 5:10, 18.
verses.commentary:
10:25 The prophet's prayer to God continues and pleads that He will judge (lit. "pour out," BDB 1049,
KB 1629, Qal IMPERATIVE) the nations (and the families) which He used to judge His people
(cf. Ps. 79:6-7). The ultimate goal of creation is to know YHWH and have a world that reflects His character.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and
the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- What metaphor or analogy does Jeremiah use in chapter 8 to describe Judah's reluctance
to repent?

- Why are the graves opened in Jeremiah 8?

- Who are the scribes in Jeremiah 8?

- Who is speaking in Jer. 8:18-9:16?

- List the judgments that God will send on Judah in Jeremiah 9.

- Describe Jeremiah's understanding of circumcision and its purpose.

- List the reasons for the futility of idolatry found in Jeremiah 10.

- List the attributes of YHWH in Jeremiah 10.

- Why did God allow His people to be exiled!

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- There is a literary unit from Jeremiah 7 through 10 which deals with Judah's sin and
YHWH's judgment (see Contextual Insighst at chapter 8, A).

- The poems of Jeremiah are arranged, not by date, but by

- word plays

- themes

- This chapter has many similarities with both Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Two examples:

- the rare word (BDB 903 I), "cucumber field," Jer. 10:5 (cf. Isa. 1:8)

- the phrase, "none is like You," Jer. 10:6 reflects Deut. 33:26 (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM)

- Prophetic literature is a genre which modern readers are not familiar with. It must be interpreted in light of

- contemporary culture

- contemporary idioms

- contemporary poetic forms

- parallel patterns

Some resources that have helped me try to put muself back into an ANE mindset are

- John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic

- G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible

- Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read the Bible for All Its Worth

1Hear the word which the Lord speaks to you, O house

of Israel.
